title: One year in Toronto · B1 checkpoint
subtitle: Un anno dopo · B1 checkpoint
intro: September again. Chiara's decision (told in the last episode), a letter to Roccamarina, a radio-style interview on a community station about the pasticciotto that sold out, and a last call with Luca / Lucia from the shop by the sea. Crossover with [[IT Unit 24]]. The B1 checkpoint: all tenses on a timeline, the complete list of false friends between Italian and English, word formation, and Canadian spelling with its US and UK notes.
objectives: Riassumere un anno di esperienze: [[a year ago I didn't speak English well]], [[now I've opened a bakery]]
Riflettere e paragonare: [[if I hadn't moved, I wouldn't have met Marcus]]
Padroneggiare i falsi amici in una lista completa
Scrivere un racconto lungo con tutti i tempi inglesi
Capire e distinguere le ortografie canadese, americana e britannica
canDo: B1 · Writing: can write a one-page English letter / email with mixed tenses, conditionals, and reported speech.
B1 · Spoken production: can summarise a year and justify decisions.
B1 · Reading: can follow a newspaper article and a short radio interview transcript.
B1 · Listening: can follow a natural-speed conversation of three or more speakers.
B1 · Checkpoint: can handle every grammar point of units 1–24 in a mixed exam.

sections.title: The letter, the interview, the call
sections.intro: Three scenes: the letter Chiara writes to Roccamarina; a Thursday-afternoon community-radio interview about the pasticciotti; the Sunday-night Zoom call with {hero} from Toronto to Roccamarina. Listen for every B1 tense in sequence.

blocks.title: The letter to Roccamarina
blocks.setting: Friday 11 September, 7 p.m., 42 Lansdowne basement kitchen. Chiara at the table with a cup of tea and two pens. On the laptop, a half-written letter addressed to Dora, Pasquale, Nando, Tommaso, and {hero}. Outside: late-summer dusk.

lines.t: «Dear everyone, a year ago today, I left Roccamarina with a suitcase and the address of my cousins in Vaughan. I had never seen the Atlantic from an airplane window. I had never worked a day for someone outside the family. I had never signed a lease on my own. By midnight on September 15 last year, I had done all three.»
lines.n: «Cari tutti, un anno fa oggi ho lasciato Roccamarina con una valigia e l'indirizzo dei miei cugini a Vaughan. Non avevo mai visto l'Atlantico dal finestrino. Non avevo mai lavorato un giorno per qualcuno fuori dalla famiglia. Non avevo mai firmato un contratto d'affitto da sola. Entro mezzanotte del 15 settembre dell'anno scorso, avevo fatto tutte e tre.»
lines.note: Three past perfects (I had never seen, worked, signed) + one past perfect in the main clause (by midnight… I had done). The whole first paragraph is a tense setup.

lines.t: «Looking back, I can tell you three things I would have done differently if I had known. One, I would have applied to Express Entry before leaving Italy. Two, I would have brought warmer clothes. Three, I would have called Dora every Sunday without waiting for her to call me. The rest I would do the same way.»
lines.n: «Guardando indietro, posso dirvi tre cose che avrei fatto diversamente se avessi saputo. Uno, avrei fatto domanda per Express Entry prima di partire. Due, avrei portato vestiti più caldi. Tre, avrei chiamato Dora ogni domenica senza aspettare che chiamasse lei. Il resto lo rifarei uguale.»
lines.note: Looking back: participle phrase opener. Three third conditionals: I would have done, applied, brought, called. The I would do the same way (second conditional).

lines.t: «I am going to stay another year. Doug has filed an employer letter for my Provincial Nominee Program file, which Priya helped me draft. The invitation might take six months, and the PR another twelve to eighteen. By the time I come back to Roccamarina for a wedding or for a Christmas, I may already have the card. I'm not holding my breath; I'm getting on with it.»
lines.n: «Rimarrò un altro anno. Doug ha depositato una lettera di datore di lavoro per la mia pratica PNP, che Priya mi ha aiutata a redigere. L'invito può richiedere sei mesi, e la PR altri 12-18. Entro quando tornerò a Roccamarina per un matrimonio o per Natale, potrei già avere la carta. Non trattengo il respiro; vado avanti.»
lines.note: I am going to stay: future with going to. Doug has filed: present perfect. Which Priya helped me draft: relative clause. The invitation might take: modal might. I'm getting on with it: get on with = continue.

lines.t: «Dora, tell Nonna Rosa that the pasticciotto has been accepted by the Blog TO food editor, who called the shop 'a small revolution of a classic Lecce pastry transplanted to the heart of Toronto'. The copy from Giulia, who writes for La Repubblica, is on its way to Dora in the mail. I'm proud of the pasticciotti, in a quiet way; I'm prouder of this year.»
lines.n: «Dora, di' a nonna Rosa che il pasticciotto è stato accettato dal food editor di Blog TO, che l'ha definito 'una piccola rivoluzione di un classico leccese trapiantato nel cuore di Toronto'. La copia di Giulia, che scrive per La Repubblica, sta arrivando a Dora per posta. Sono orgogliosa dei pasticciotti, in modo tranquillo; sono più orgogliosa di quest'anno.»
lines.note: Has been accepted by: present perfect passive. Who called the shop: relative clause. On its way: idiom. I'm prouder: comparative.

lines.t: «Pasquale, I started saying 'eh?' at the end of my questions. Don't tell me the Macarena was an obstacle to Italian citizenship; I'll give it up. — I'll pay for a pasticciotto for whoever reads this letter aloud at the Bar Centrale. The money is already with Nando's cousin at the BCC. Love, Chiara.»
lines.n: «Pasquale, ho iniziato a dire 'eh?' alla fine delle mie domande. Non dirmi che il Macarena era un ostacolo alla cittadinanza italiana; lo abbandonerò. — Pago un pasticciotto a chi legge questa lettera a voce alta al Bar Centrale. I soldi sono già dal cugino di Nando alla BCC. Un abbraccio, Chiara.»
lines.note: I started saying 'eh?': start + -ing. For whoever reads: whoever + 3rd person sing. The money is already with Nando's cousin: present + possessive with 's.

notes.phrase: I had never seen · I had never worked · I had never signed · by midnight I had done · if I had known, I would have applied · I'm going to stay · has been accepted · for whoever reads
notes.note: Every B1 tense in one letter: past perfect, 3rd conditional, future going to, present perfect passive, whoever + 3rd sing.

blocks.title: The radio interview
blocks.setting: Thursday 17 September, 2:15 p.m., CIUT 89.5 FM community radio, University of Toronto, Hart House basement. A ten-minute food segment on The Dish, hosted by Marta Jurkiewicz. Chiara in the booth with headphones. Her first Toronto radio interview, three minutes of pre-prep and one printed sheet of English quotes.
blocks.register: informal interview, with the formal register of radio

lines.t: You're listening to The Dish on CIUT 89.5. Today I'm joined by Chiara Russo, who's been running the pasticciotto program at Doug's Bakery on College for the past year. Chiara, welcome. — Thanks, Marta. — Tell us: what is a pasticciotto, and how did you end up making 300 of them a Saturday morning in Toronto?
lines.n: State ascoltando The Dish su CIUT 89.5. Oggi sono con me Chiara Russo, che gestisce il programma pasticciotto da Doug's Bakery su College da un anno. Chiara, benvenuta. — Grazie, Marta. — Dicci: cos'è un pasticciotto, e come sei finita a farne 300 un sabato mattina a Toronto?
lines.note: The radio opener. You're listening to: present continuous for a describable current state. Who's been running: present perfect continuous. How did you end up: end up + -ing for the result.

lines.t: A pasticciotto is a small shortcrust pastry filled with vanilla custard, baked for exactly nine minutes, best eaten at six in the morning with a strong espresso. It's from Lecce, in Puglia, in the south-east of Italy. The classic recipe is almost 300 years old. Mine, at Doug's, is a direct copy of my grandmother's version. — So — a 300-year-old pastry, baked by a 27-year-old, in a bakery owned by a 72-year-old. How did that happen?
lines.n: Un pasticciotto è una piccola pasta frolla ripiena di crema pasticcera alla vaniglia, cotta per nove minuti esatti, meglio mangiata alle sei del mattino con un espresso forte. Viene da Lecce, in Puglia, nel sud-est dell'Italia. La ricetta classica ha quasi 300 anni. La mia, da Doug, è una copia diretta della versione di mia nonna. — Allora — una pasta di 300 anni, cotta da una 27enne, in una pasticceria di proprietà di un 72enne. Come è successo?
lines.note: A small shortcrust pastry filled with vanilla custard: participle phrase as modifier. In a bakery owned by: passive participle as modifier. The compact register of radio.

lines.t: I arrived last September on a Working Holiday permit. Doug, who runs the bakery, had hired a girl two years earlier, who had lasted three weeks. He was more cautious this time. I started washing dishes. By December, I was baking shortbread. By March, I was running the pasticciotti. Priya, the manager, said: 'You bring something no one else does, and the dough knows'. — The dough knows. That's a line.
lines.n: Sono arrivata a settembre scorso con un permesso Working Holiday. Doug, che gestisce la panetteria, aveva assunto una ragazza due anni prima, che era durata tre settimane. Era più cauto questa volta. Ho iniziato lavando i piatti. Entro dicembre, cuocevo il shortbread. Entro marzo, gestivo i pasticciotti. Priya, la manager, mi disse: 'Porti qualcosa che nessun altro porta, e l'impasto lo sa'. — L'impasto lo sa. Che frase.
lines.note: Had hired a girl two years earlier, who had lasted three weeks: double past perfect with non-defining relative. Started washing dishes: start + -ing. By December, I was baking: by + time + past continuous.

lines.t: If you hadn't come to Toronto, where would you have gone? — I think I'd be in Rome, maybe, trying to open a shop. If I had stayed in Roccamarina, I'd probably be helping my cousin run her workshop. I don't know. I'm glad I came here. — You can hear the softening of the Italian accent — six months ago it was stronger. Was that intentional? — No. The accent softens on its own; it has nothing to do with intention. I still say «water» with an r and my a is still open. — You still have the pasticciotto accent. — I will always have the pasticciotto accent.
lines.n: Se non fossi venuta a Toronto, dove saresti andata? — Credo che sarei a Roma, forse, cercando di aprire un negozio. Se fossi rimasta a Roccamarina, probabilmente aiuterei mia cugina a gestire l'officina. Non lo so. Sono contenta di essere venuta qui. — Si sente l'ammorbidirsi dell'accento italiano — sei mesi fa era più forte. Era intenzionale? — No. L'accento si ammorbidisce da solo; non c'entra con l'intenzione. Dico ancora «water» con la r e la mia a è ancora aperta. — Hai ancora l'accento del pasticciotto. — Avrò sempre l'accento del pasticciotto.
lines.note: Third conditional + mixed conditional in response. If you hadn't come, where would you have gone? If I had stayed, I'd be helping. The pasticciotto accent: a joke.

lines.t: The Dish was back from the pasticciotto corner of the world. Chiara Russo, baker at Doug's. The pasticciotti are at Doug's Bakery on College — the address is on our website. Come back and see us when the sfogliatelle arrive. — I will.
lines.n: The Dish torna dal pasticciotto corner del mondo. Chiara Russo, fornaia da Doug. I pasticciotti si trovano da Doug's Bakery su College — l'indirizzo è sul nostro sito. Torna quando arrivano le sfogliatelle. — Lo farò.
lines.note: The classic radio closer. On our website: location. Come back and see us when: when + present for a future habit (zero conditional).

notes.phrase: a pastry filled with vanilla custard, baked for nine minutes, best eaten at six · a bakery owned by a 72-year-old · Doug, who runs the bakery, had hired a girl who had lasted three weeks · I started washing · by December I was baking · if I hadn't come, where would I have gone
notes.note: Every B1 structure in one three-minute radio interview.

blocks.title: The Sunday-night call to Roccamarina
blocks.setting: Sunday 20 September, 9:15 p.m. Toronto time, 3:15 a.m. Monday in Roccamarina. {hero} on video with Chiara. Four thousand five hundred kilometres apart. Both of them standing in their respective kitchens. Each with a tea.

lines.t: You read your letter? Dora read it aloud to the whole Bar Centrale at noon on Thursday. There was a line of people from the pharmacy to the butcher's listening in. Franca cried; Pasquale cried; Nando pretended not to cry; I cried. — You're kidding. — I'm not. — I'm going to charge all of you for the pasticciotti.
lines.n: Hai letto la tua lettera? Dora l'ha letta a voce alta a tutto il Bar Centrale a mezzogiorno di giovedì. C'era una fila dalla farmacia al macellaio in ascolto. Franca ha pianto; Pasquale ha pianto; Nando ha finto di non piangere; io ho pianto. — Scherzi. — No. — Vi fatturerò tutti i pasticciotti.
lines.note: Charming, concrete, in the past simple + a joke in the future.

lines.t: {hero}. I have to ask — now that it's a year — do you think I'd be the same person if I hadn't moved? — No. You'd be the Chiara we knew. Not better, not worse — just the version that stayed. You've become someone new, and we love her too. Both of you.
lines.n: {hero}. Devo chiederti — ora che è un anno — pensi che sarei la stessa persona se non mi fossi trasferita? — No. Saresti la Chiara che conoscevamo. Non meglio, non peggio — solo la versione che è rimasta. Sei diventata una nuova, e vogliamo bene anche a lei. Ad entrambe.
lines.note: Mixed conditional: I'd be the same person if I hadn't moved. You've become: present perfect for a result-still-true. Both of you: direct address, singular + plural.

lines.t: Doug told me yesterday that if he had met me at twenty, he would've trained me to take over sooner. He's 72; the bakery is tired like him. I'm going to buy a 10% share in January. It's a small step. He wrote it into the employer letter so IRCC knows I have a stake.
lines.n: Doug mi ha detto ieri che se mi avesse conosciuto a vent'anni, mi avrebbe formata a prendere il controllo prima. Ha 72 anni; la panetteria è stanca come lui. Comprerò una quota del 10% a gennaio. È un piccolo passo. L'ha scritto nella lettera di datore di lavoro così IRCC sa che ho una partecipazione.
lines.note: Doug told me yesterday that if he had met me at twenty, he would've trained me: reported 3rd conditional (he said, if he had met me, he would've). I'm going to buy: future with going to.

lines.t: I'll meet you at the airport this December with a sign and a toque. — I'll be wearing my own toque by then, {hero}. Don't bring one. Bring Dora, Pasquale, Nando, and the whole Corso. — I'll see what I can do.
lines.n: Ti vengo a prendere all'aeroporto a dicembre con un cartello e un berretto. — A quell'ora avrò già il mio berretto, {hero}. Non portarlo. Porta Dora, Pasquale, Nando, e tutto il Corso. — Vedo cosa posso fare.
lines.note: I'll meet you at the airport: future with will. I'll be wearing my own toque by then: future continuous (will + be + -ing). I'll see what I can do: future.

notes.phrase: if I hadn't moved · if he had met me at twenty · I'll be wearing · I'm going to buy · you've become · both of you
notes.note: Every B1 structure, including the future continuous introduced here (I'll be wearing).

questions.q: «By midnight on September 15, I had done all three» means:
options: All three actions were complete by midnight on September 15 (past perfect for completion by a past time).
I usually do all three by midnight.
questions.why: Past perfect for an action complete before a past reference point (midnight).

questions.q: «If I hadn't come to Toronto, where would you have gone?» is a 3rd conditional.
questions.why: If + past perfect + would have + part.

questions.q: A year ago I ___ (not speak, imp.) English well. I ___ (never, work, past perfect) at a bakery. Today I ___ (be, pres.) a baker. In a year I ___ (have, fut. perf.) PR, maybe.
questions.n: Un anno fa non parlavo bene l'inglese. Non avevo mai lavorato in pasticceria. Oggi sono fornaia. Entro un anno avrò la PR, forse.

sections.title: A year in words
sections.intro: Four themes: reflection and change, life abroad, plans and uncertainty, and the complete list of false friends between Italian and English with a short glossary of 2026-era Canadian English.

ex.t: I've grown into the person Priya saw in me a year ago.
ex.n: Sono cresciuta nella persona che Priya ha visto in me un anno fa.

items.note: Grow + into: become. Also grow apart, grow up.

ex.t: I've settled into the basement apartment, finally.
ex.n: Mi sono finalmente sistemata nel seminterrato.

items.note: Also settle down. From unit 20.

ex.t: I belong here, and I belong there, and that is a possible answer.
ex.n: Appartengo qui, e appartengo lì, e questa è una risposta possibile.

items.note: Belong to + place / person. Also a sense of belonging.

ex.t: A sense of belonging I had never felt in Rome.
ex.n: Un senso di appartenenza che non avevo mai sentito a Roma.

items.note: Common idiom, both abstract and practical.

ex.t: Looking back, I would have called Dora every Sunday.
ex.n: Guardando indietro, avrei chiamato Dora ogni domenica.

items.note: Participle phrase opener. Also look ahead / look forward.

ex.t: I've come to terms with being far from home.
ex.n: Ho fatto pace con l'essere lontana da casa.

items.note: Come to terms with + noun / -ing.

ex.t: The first year abroad is a milestone, not a destination.
ex.n: Il primo anno all'estero è una pietra miliare, non un arrivo.

items.note: Also informally: a big step. From medieval road markers.

ex.t: A year is a good moment to take stock.
ex.n: Un anno è un buon momento per fare un bilancio.

items.note: Idiom from merchant inventory.

ex.t: With hindsight, I would have applied earlier.
ex.n: Con il senno di poi, avrei fatto domanda prima.

items.note: The ability to understand after the event. Hindsight is 20/20: a classic phrase.

ex.t: Toronto has 60,000 newcomers a year.
ex.n: Toronto ha 60.000 nuovi arrivati all'anno.

items.note: Newcomer is the preferred term in Canadian official English; immigrant is still common.

ex.t: A PR card is good for five years at a time.
ex.n: Una PR card dura cinque anni alla volta.

items.note: From unit 20. Also landed immigrant (older term).

ex.t: Canadian citizenship: 3 years of PR + 2026 test.
ex.n: Cittadinanza canadese: 3 anni di PR + test del 2026.

items.note: Dual citizenship: standard. Italo-Canadian: a common configuration.

ex.t: The citizenship oath, taken in English and French.
ex.n: Il giuramento di cittadinanza, in inglese e francese.

items.note: Take the oath. Standard final step of the citizenship process.

ex.t: Spousal sponsorship: 2-year commitment.
ex.n: Sponsorship coniugale: 2 anni di impegno.

items.note: From unit 20. Both verb and noun forms.

ex.t: YMCA settlement workers help newcomers for the first year.
ex.n: Gli assistenti di insediamento della YMCA aiutano i nuovi arrivati per il primo anno.

items.note: Settlement services: free federal help for newcomers (English classes, housing, job search).

ex.t: Canadian integration is a two-way street, officially.
ex.n: L'integrazione canadese è una strada a doppio senso, ufficialmente.

items.note: Canadian Multiculturalism Act 1988. The policy of a mosaic.

ex.t: I'll naturalise in late 2029, if the timeline holds.
ex.n: Mi naturalizzerò a fine 2029, se la tempistica regge.

items.note: Canadian spelling (unit 18): naturalise. The formal verb for 'become a citizen'.

ex.t: The oath of allegiance to Canada and the Crown.
ex.n: Il giuramento di fedeltà al Canada e alla Corona.

items.note: Required by law; wording set by the Citizenship Act.

ex.t: Canada doesn't ask you to assimilate; it asks you to add.
ex.n: Il Canada non ti chiede di assimilarti; ti chiede di aggiungere.

items.note: A key difference between Canadian and US-style policies.

blocks.theme: False friends IT ↔ EN · the full list

ex.t: Actually, I'm Italian — not Canadian. Attualmente = currently (right now).
ex.n: In realtà, sono italiana — non canadese. Attualmente = adesso, al momento.

items.note: Classic false friend. Italian attualmente = currently; English actually = in reality.

ex.t: I'll eventually get PR. Eventualmente = possibly, maybe.
ex.n: Alla fine prenderò la PR. Eventualmente = possibly.

items.note: English eventually = in the end; Italian eventualmente = possibly / in case.

ex.t: A sensible decision. Sensibile = sensitive (emotionally or to touch).
ex.n: Una decisione ragionevole. Sensibile = sensitive, suscettibile.

items.note: A classic. Sensible = reasonable; sensitive = emotionally alert.

ex.t: The Lillian H. Smith Library on College. Libreria = bookshop.
ex.n: La biblioteca Lillian H. Smith su College. Libreria = negozio di libri.

items.note: The tax clinic in unit 22 is at a library (biblioteca), not a bookshop.

ex.t: A factory worker in Hamilton. Fattoria = farm.
ex.n: Un operaio di fabbrica a Hamilton. Fattoria = fattoria agricola.

items.note: The Italo-Canadian word fattoria for factory is italiese; standard Italian: fabbrica.

ex.t: My parents are coming to Toronto for Christmas. Parenti = relatives.
ex.n: I miei genitori vengono a Toronto per Natale. Parenti = relatives.

items.note: Classic classroom mix-up.

ex.t: A sympathetic listener. Simpatico = likeable, friendly.
ex.n: Un ascoltatore comprensivo. Simpatico = simpatico (person).

items.note: English sympathetic = understanding; Italian simpatico = pleasant.

ex.t: No preservatives in Doug's bread.
ex.n: Nessun conservante nel pane di Doug.

items.note: A famous false friend. Preservative = conservante; preservativo = condom (very different).

ex.t: A morbid sense of humour. Morbido = soft (touch).
ex.n: Un umorismo macabro. Morbido = soft, come la seta.

items.note: English morbid = unhealthy preoccupation; Italian morbido = soft.

ex.t: I had an argument with my cousin. Argomento = topic.
ex.n: Ho avuto una discussione con mio cugino. Argomento = topic.

items.note: English argument = quarrel; Italian argomento = topic / subject matter.

ex.t: A comprehensive guide to Canadian taxes. Comprensivo = understanding (person).
ex.n: Una guida completa alle tasse canadesi. Comprensivo = una persona comprensiva.

items.note: English comprehensive = complete; Italian comprensivo = sympathetic / understanding.

items.n: educated = istruito (= having studied); educato = polite

ex.t: She's an educated woman. — Dog è un cane ben educato (polite dog).
ex.n: È una donna istruita. — Il cane è ben educato (polite).

items.note: Different roots. English educated = formally educated; Italian educato = well-mannered.

ex.t: The estate of my grandfather. Estate = summer.
ex.n: Il patrimonio di mio nonno. Estate = season of summer.

items.note: Estate in English can mean an inheritance, a large property, or a legal entity.

ex.t: A fabric store on Queen West. Fabbrica = factory.
ex.n: Un negozio di tessuti su Queen West. Fabbrica = factory.

items.note: English fabric = cloth; Italian fabbrica = factory.

ex.t: A rumour went around. — Un rumore in cucina.
ex.n: Una voce / diceria. — Un rumore in cucina.

items.note: English rumour = voce; Italian rumore = noise.

ex.t: A terrific pasticciotto!
ex.n: Un pasticciotto fantastico!

items.note: English terrific = great; terrifying = frightening. Different words.

ex.t: A lunatic driver. Lunatico = moody.
ex.n: Un conducente pazzo. Lunatico = volubile.

items.note: English lunatic = insane; Italian lunatico = moody / changeable.

ex.t: The New Yorker magazine. Magazzino = warehouse.
ex.n: La rivista New Yorker. Magazzino = magazzino di stoccaggio.

items.note: English magazine = rivista; Italian magazzino = warehouse / shop stock.

ex.t: A new camera. Camera = room.
ex.n: Una macchina fotografica nuova. Camera = stanza.

items.note: English camera = macchina fotografica; Italian camera = room (unit 2).

ex.t: A brave decision. Bravo = good (at X).
ex.n: Una decisione coraggiosa. Bravo = capace, abile.

items.note: English brave = courageous; Italian bravo = good (at something, or saying well done).

ex.t: I was annoyed by the delay. Annoiato = bored.
ex.n: Ero irritata per il ritardo. Annoiato = bored.

items.note: English annoyed = irritated; Italian annoiato = bored.

ex.t: The weather is cold. — Il tempo è caldo.
ex.n: Fa freddo. — Fa caldo.

items.note: The classic false friend by homophony — cold vs caldo. Different meanings entirely.

ex.t: The editor of the magazine. Editore = publisher.
ex.n: Il redattore della rivista. Editore = casa editrice / editore.

items.note: English editor = who edits; Italian editore = publishing house / publisher.

items.n: attend = partecipare, non 'attendere'; pretend = fingere, non 'pretendere'

ex.t: I attended the ceremony (attended = partecipato).
ex.n: Ho partecipato alla cerimonia. Non: ho atteso.

items.note: Attend = to go to (an event / school); pretend = to feign. Italian attendere = to wait; pretendere = to demand.

items.n: confront = affrontare, non 'confrontare'; assist = aiutare, non 'assistere'; convenient = comodo, non 'conveniente'

ex.t: She confronted him. He assisted me. The time is convenient.
ex.n: Lo ha affrontato. Mi ha aiutata. L'ora è comoda.

items.note: Three more pairs. Italian confrontare = to compare; assistere = to witness; conveniente = inexpensive.

ex.t: Casual dress. Casuale = random.
ex.n: Vestito informale. Casuale = random, by chance.

items.note: English casual = informal; Italian casuale = by chance.

ex.t: Watch the pavement. Pavimento = floor.
ex.n: Attenta al marciapiede. Pavimento = floor.

items.note: English pavement = sidewalk; Italian pavimento = floor.

ex.t: Buy a stamp at the post office. Stampa = print / press.
ex.n: Compra un francobollo alle poste. Stampa = print.

items.note: English stamp = francobollo; Italian stampa = print / the press.

ex.t: A job vacancy at Doug's. Vacanza = holiday.
ex.n: Un posto vacante da Doug. Vacanza = ferie.

items.note: English vacancy = empty position (job, room); Italian vacanza = holiday.

ex.t: A Rosedale mansion. Mansione = task.
ex.n: Una villa a Rosedale. Mansione = task.

items.note: English mansion = big fancy house; Italian mansione = duty / role.

ex.t: A 400-page novel. Novella = short story / tale.
ex.n: Un romanzo di 400 pagine. Novella = racconto breve.

sections.title: B1 on one screen
sections.intro: Three pieces: the English tense timeline map (all tenses on one grid), word formation (prefixes and suffixes), and the full false-friend awareness.

blocks.title: The tense timeline
blocks.rule: The twelve English tenses (plus the conditional perfect) on one grid. Simple: present (I write), past (I wrote), future (I will write). Continuous: present cont. (I am writing), past cont. (I was writing), future cont. (I will be writing). Perfect: present perfect (I have written), past perfect (I had written), future perfect (I will have written). Perfect continuous: present perfect cont. (I have been writing), past perfect cont. (I had been writing), future perfect cont. (I will have been writing). Conditional / third conditional: I would write / I would have written. On the time axis: past perfect → past simple → present → future simple → future perfect. On the aspect axis: simple (fact) / continuous (in progress) / perfect (completed with current relevance). B1 uses all of them.

items.t: I wrote a letter yesterday. I was writing when the phone rang. I have written three drafts. I had written two drafts before noon.
items.n: Ho scritto una lettera ieri. Stavo scrivendo quando è squillato il telefono. Ho scritto tre bozze. Avevo scritto due bozze prima di mezzogiorno.

items.t: I will write a report tomorrow. I will be writing all afternoon. I will have written it by Friday. I'd write more if I had time.
items.n: Scriverò un report domani. Starò scrivendo tutto il pomeriggio. L'avrò scritto entro venerdì. Ne scriverei di più se avessi tempo.

blocks.title: Word formation: prefixes and suffixes
blocks.rule: Three groups of word-forming parts. Prefixes change meaning: un- (unhappy, unlock, unlike); dis- (dislike, dishonest, disappear); re- (rebuild, reopen, re-use); in-/im-/il-/ir- (inactive, impossible, illegal, irregular); mis- (misunderstand, misread); over- (overdo, oversleep); under- (undercook, underline); pre- (prepay, preschool); post- (postwar, postgraduate); self- (self-made, self-service). Suffixes change part of speech. Noun: -ness (kindness, happiness), -ment (improvement, agreement), -ity (ability, security), -tion (nation, education), -ship (friendship, membership), -hood (childhood, neighbourhood). Adjective: -ful (helpful, careful), -less (helpless, careless), -ous (famous, dangerous), -y (sunny, rainy), -able / -ible (readable, visible), -ive (active, creative). Adverb: -ly (quickly, carefully — not: friendly, which is an adjective). Verb: -ise / -ize (realize, modernise), -en (strengthen, deepen). Learn these as a system: unhappy + -ness = unhappiness; care + -less + -ly = carelessly; create + -ive + -ity = creativity.

Creates

items.t: unhappy (un + happy); unhappiness (un + happy + ness); carelessly (care + less + ly); creativity (create + ive + ity).
Priya is a thoughtful person (thought + ful). Mateo is thoughtless about dishes (thought + less). Chiara's work has been full of thoughtfulness this year (thought + ful + ness).
items.n: Priya è premurosa. Mateo è disattento. Il lavoro di Chiara è stato pieno di premura quest'anno.

blocks.title: Top errors Italians make in English
blocks.rule: Thirty errors to avoid at B1. (1) Agreement with -s: he goes, she goes, Chiara goes. (2) Do / does in questions and negatives: Do you work? She doesn't live here. (3) Articles: a / an / the / zero — different distribution than Italian (I speak Italian, not «I speak the Italian»). (4) Prepositions of place: in Toronto, at the airport, on the subway. (5) Prepositions of time: in July, on Monday, at 7, from… to… (6) Future: will vs going to vs present continuous. (7) Past simple vs present perfect: I lived in Rome vs I have lived in Toronto for a year. (8) For / since: for + duration, since + point. (9) Tag questions: isn't she? doesn't he? (10) The passive: is checked / was checked / has been checked. (11) Reported speech backshift: he said he was tired (not he said he is tired). (12) Say vs tell: say that, tell someone that. (13) Modal verbs: must / have to / should / might. (14) Conditional types: if + past → would; if + past perfect → would have. (15) Relative clauses: who / which / that / whose / where. (16) Gerund vs infinitive after verbs: enjoy baking vs decide to bake. (17) Phrasal verbs: look up, pick up, turn off, break down. (18) Preposition at the end of a question: Who are you talking to? (19) False friends: actually, eventually, library, parents. (20) -ing vs -ed adjectives: boring (thing) vs bored (person). (21) Much / many: much + uncountable, many + countable. (22) Little / few: little + uncountable (little time), few + countable (few friends). (23) Comparative: -er or more + adjective. (24) Superlative: the -est or the most + adjective. (25) Would like vs want: I would like a coffee (polite), I want a coffee (direct). (26) Possessive 's: Chiara's book, not «the book of Chiara». (27) Would of / could of / should of (misspelling of would have). (28) It's vs its: it's = it is; its = possessive. (29) Who / whom in formal writing: who (subject), whom (object). (30) Comma splices in writing: use a semicolon or a conjunction, not just a comma.

blocks.title: The diagnostic passage
blocks.text: Read slowly, record yourself, listen back: [[A year ago, Chiara arrived in Toronto with a suitcase, three thousand euros and the address of her cousins. She hadn't thought about Canadian winters; the eighteenth of January she borrowed Teresa's parka and never gave it back. By March, she was baking pasticciotti at six in the morning, before the sun was fully up. She says the dough knows when you're honest; she says the city knows too. She might be right; she's been right about most things this year. (pause) If she had stayed in Lecce, we wouldn't be meeting her at Pearson next December with a sign.]] Nine features in one paragraph. If you can read it aloud with ease, your B1 pronunciation is in shape.

items.n: Dora farà i cartellati per Natale. Chiara farà la scelta berretto / parka. Marcus e Priya faranno un viaggio in Italia il prossimo anno. Doug guadagnerà molto se i pasticciotti si vendono.

items.q: Write a one-page letter to a friend abroad summarising a year of your life in English, using at least: three different tenses (past simple, present perfect, past perfect), one 3rd conditional, one participle phrase (looking back / having spent), one reported speech sentence (he said that he…), one false friend used correctly (actually, eventually, library…), one Canadian spelling word (colour, centre, favourite, programme, travelled), and the two formulas 'a year ago' and 'today'.
items.model: Dear [friend], a year ago today I arrived in Toronto with a suitcase. I had never worked at a bakery, I had never signed a lease, I had never seen the Atlantic from the air. Today I have done all three, which is the point of a year. Looking back, I would have applied to Express Entry before leaving Rome, but I didn't actually know what Express Entry was — I thought a Working Holiday permit was the whole deal. The baker, Doug, has filed an employer letter for my PNP file, which Priya helped me draft, and which should move me closer to a PR card by next summer. I had an argument with my parents in April, when they said I would eventually come home; I told them that Canada was not a long holiday but a possible home. Dora, meanwhile, has been teaching me — in weekly phone calls — the Salento recipes my grandmother never wrote down, which have travelled to my favourite kitchen in Bloordale. I will come back for Christmas, in a borrowed parka that is bigger than me, with a one-euro bottle of amaro, and a story. All my love, Chiara.
items.hint: Dear [friend], a year ago today I arrived… · I had never… · Today I have done all three · Looking back, I would have… · I had an argument with my parents, when they said I would eventually… · Dora has been teaching me… · my favourite kitchen · I will come back for Christmas · All my love.

sections.title: PR, the citizenship test, Italo-Canadian identity, where to go next
sections.intro: Four pages: the path from PR to citizenship, the Italo-Canadian identity in detail, the question of staying or returning, and the next steps in English (IELTS, CELPIP, Cambridge).

blocks.text: The Canadian path (in 2026): [[Permanent Residency]] (PR) through one of the paths of unit 20 (Express Entry, PNP, Spousal, Study + PGWP, Startup Visa). Once PR, you must be [[physically present in Canada for 1,095 days in the previous 5 years]] (730 for citizenship in some older cases). You apply for [[citizenship]] through IRCC, pay 630 CAD, and wait 12-24 months. The [[citizenship test]] has 20 questions on Canadian history, geography, government and rights (Discover Canada is the free study guide, 68 pages, PDF on IRCC). Pass at 15/20 or more. The [[citizenship oath]], in English and French, is taken at a ceremony with a Citizenship Judge. You can keep your original citizenship (Italy allows dual). Chiara's timeline, if everything goes right: PR card by late 2027; eligibility for citizenship late 2029; oath in 2030. The waiting is the hard part; the paperwork is manageable.

There are [[1.5 million]] Canadians of Italian heritage, out of 40 million Canadians total — around 3.7%, mostly concentrated in the GTA (around 500,000), Montréal (around 250,000), and metro Vancouver (around 100,000). The main waves: pre-1914 (to Montréal and the mines), 1946-1960 (mass post-war immigration from the South to Toronto, Montréal, Hamilton), 1960-1980 (continued, including the Ferrantes' generation from Veneto in Chiara's family), and 2000-present (highly educated young Italians to Toronto, Montréal and increasingly Alberta). The three generations: [[first]] (born in Italy, Italian + regional dialect at home, work in construction / manufacturing / small business), [[second]] (born in Canada, Italian at home but mostly English, white-collar professions, suburban), [[third]] (born in Canada, English only, Italo-Canadian cultural identity through food / weddings / grandparents / soccer, mixed marriages increasingly common). Chiara is first-wave at twenty-seven; her cousin's children will be second. The identity is persistent: the second generation moves away from Little Italy on College Street, but Woodbridge preserves it; the third generation returns to the city, often for university at Toronto, Guelph or Western. The [[Columbus Centre]] in North York is the civic heart; the [[Italian Cultural Institute]] at the Consulate on St Clair is the official one; the [[Taste of Little Italy]] festival in June and the [[Mondo Italiano festival]] in Woodbridge are the public ones.

blocks.title: To stay or to return · the quiet question
blocks.text: Most of the 2000-present Italian wave stays in Canada; a quieter minority (around 30%, according to AIRE back-flows) returns to Italy within 10 years, usually because of family, climate, cost of living, or a specific opportunity. The returners often say the same four things: [[I missed the sea]]; [[I missed the sun]]; [[my parents aged]]; [[the Canadian salary didn't translate to Italian cost of living once I added the taxes and the family support I don't need there]]. The stayers say: [[professional opportunity]]; [[healthcare]]; [[safety]]; [[the children's education]]; [[a social contract that works, even when imperfect]]. Chiara is a stayer, for now, with a return-by-December promise and a 10% bakery stake. If this were a different story, she would be a returner by 2030, like one of her high-school friends from Lecce who went to Berlin for seven years and now runs a pastry shop in Taranto with the German efficiency and the Puglian recipes.

Three directions after B1 in English. (1) [[Certifications]]: [[IELTS]] (standard worldwide), [[CELPIP]] (Canadian-specific, more useful for immigration), [[Cambridge]] (FCE / CAE / CPE / BEC for business), [[TOEFL]] (US-focused). For Canadian immigration, CELPIP General or IELTS General. For UK and Australian immigration, IELTS General. For university entry, IELTS Academic or TOEFL. CLB levels: CLB 4 = IELTS 4; CLB 7 = IELTS 6.0; CLB 9 = IELTS 7.0. (2) [[B2 content]]: longer reading (The Walrus, The Economist, The Globe and Mail), long-form writing (essays, cover letters), the simple-past subjunctive (if I were, if she were) more fluently, advanced phrasal verbs, formal academic register, Canadian cultural referentials (Margaret Atwood, Alice Munro, Michael Ondaatje, Dionne Brand). (3) [[Lived English]]: the next unit is not learned, it's spoken. Volunteer, join a tandem partner, work in English for a year, read a Canadian book club selection, watch Schitt's Creek with the subtitles off. The grammar is in your pocket; the register is in the ear. If you want to formalise, the [[Toronto Public Library]] has free CELPIP prep courses; [[Access Alliance]] runs free English classes at CLB 1-6 for newcomers. If you want to go deeper, apply to a Canadian university (admission at CLB 7-8, higher for programs that use writing extensively).
